title: Personality disorder
blurb: Care for people with borderline (emotionally unstable) personality disorder in line with NICE CG78: hope, consistency, crisis plans, the right therapy and minimal medication.
question: Leah, 24, with borderline personality disorder, attends A&E after cutting her arm for the third time this month. A staff member says she is 'attention seeking' and should not be seen by mental health services because of her diagnosis. What does NICE say?

teach.body: Borderline personality disorder (BPD), also called emotionally unstable personality disorder, is a long-term pattern of intense, rapidly changing emotions, unstable relationships and self-image, impulsivity, fear of abandonment and often repeated self-harm. Many people have experienced rejection, abuse or trauma. In plain English: emotions hit harder and faster and are hard to calm, and relationships can swing between closeness and rejection. Recovery is possible.

head: Principle
In practice
rows: Not excluded from any service because of the diagnosis or self-harm
Explain that recovery is possible and attainable
Many have faced rejection, abuse, trauma and stigma
Ask if the person wants them involved; with consent
Plan and phase transitions; strong reactions are expected
teach.caption: CG78 1.1.1.1, 1.1.3.1, 1.1.4.1, 1.1.6.1, 1.1.8.

rows.label: Purpose
values: Drugs for BPD itself or its symptoms

rows.label: In a crisis
values: One sedative short term, e.g. antihistamine

rows.label: Duration
values: Plan to stop, usually within 1 week

teach.body: Psychological therapy is the main treatment, within a structured, team-based service with supervision. For women with BPD for whom reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority, consider a comprehensive dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) programme. Outside a structured service of this kind, do not use brief psychological interventions (less than 3 months) specifically for BPD or its individual symptoms. Twice-weekly sessions may be considered.

steps.label: Calm, non-threatening
steps.sub: See it from the person's view

steps.label: Validate and explore
steps.sub: Empathic open questions; do not minimise

steps.label: Alternatives before admission
steps.sub: Crisis resolution and home treatment first

steps.label: Follow-up agreed
steps.sub: Time frame agreed with the person

teach.body: People with BPD often meet stigma: being called 'manipulative' or 'attention seeking'. Distress is real and self-harm needs care, not judgement. 'Splitting' describes seeing some staff as all good and others as all bad, which can divide a team. The response is a consistent, agreed team approach, clear boundaries delivered warmly, honest communication and supervision for staff (CG78 1.1.8.2).

Nurse Adams challenges the comment kindly: NICE says people with BPD must not be excluded from services because of their diagnosis or self-harm. She treats Leah's wound with the same care as any other, speaks calmly, validates her distress, and asks what led to tonight. She consults Leah's crisis plan, arranges a psychosocial assessment under NG225, and avoids promising solutions before she understands the problem.

teach.text: Do not treat BPD with long-term antipsychotics or a cocktail of drugs: NICE says no drug treatment for BPD itself. A crisis sedative is short term (usually stopped within 1 week). And brief therapy under 3 months is not used for BPD outside a structured, supervised BPD service.

items: Never exclude people from services because of a BPD diagnosis or self-harm.
Hope, trust, trauma awareness, consistency and carefully planned endings.
No drugs for BPD itself; crisis sedative short term, usually stopped within 1 week.
Consider comprehensive DBT for women where reducing self-harm is a priority; no brief therapy under 3 months outside a structured service.
Crisis: use the plan, validate, alternatives before admission; CPA review if admitted twice in 6 months.

summary: You can now apply NICE CG78 principles of access, hope and consistency for people with borderline personality disorder. You know the limited role of medication, when DBT is considered and how to respond in a crisis.

A.q: What does NICE CG78 say about drug treatment for borderline personality disorder?
options: Antipsychotics are first-line long-term treatment
Mood stabilisers should be offered to everyone
Drugs should not be used for BPD itself
SSRIs should be offered for emotional instability
A.why: CG78 1.3.5.1: drug treatment should not be used specifically for BPD or its individual symptoms or behaviours. Comorbid conditions may be treated.

whyNot.0: CG78 1.3.5.2: antipsychotics should not be used for medium- or long-term treatment of BPD.
whyNot.1: No drug is recommended for BPD itself.
whyNot.3: Emotional instability is a BPD symptom and drugs are not used specifically for it.

A.q: Which therapy does NICE suggest considering for women with BPD for whom reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority?
options: Comprehensive DBT programme
Six sessions of counselling
EMDR for past trauma
Brief solution-focused therapy
A.why: CG78 1.3.4.5: for women with BPD for whom reducing recurrent self-harm is a priority, consider a comprehensive dialectical behaviour therapy programme.

whyNot.1: Six sessions of counselling is a brief intervention, which CG78 1.3.4.4 advises against for BPD outside a structured service; DBT is the named option.
whyNot.2: EMDR is a PTSD treatment, not the CG78 option here.
whyNot.3: Brief solution-focused work is not the CG78 option; comprehensive DBT is named for reducing recurrent self-harm in women.

A.q: A short-term sedative is started for a person with BPD in crisis. When does NICE expect it usually to be stopped?
options: After 3 months
Within 1 week
After 6 weeks
When discharged
A.why: CG78 1.3.7.4: after a crisis, plan to stop drug treatment begun during the crisis, usually within 1 week, with regular review if it cannot be stopped.

whyNot.0: Three months is far longer than NICE intends for crisis medication.
whyNot.2: Six weeks is longer than NICE intends.
whyNot.3: Stopping is planned by time and need, not tied to discharge.

B.q: Ellie, 30, with BPD, rings the crisis line feeling overwhelmed after an argument. What should the nurse do first?
options: Arrange immediate inpatient admission
Offer solutions straight away to end the call
Use her crisis plan and listen to her view
Tell her the distress is a behavioural choice
B.why: CG78 1.3.7.1: consult the crisis plan, stay calm, understand the crisis from the person's point of view and explore reasons for distress before offering solutions.

whyNot.0: Explore other options before considering admission.
whyNot.1: NICE says refrain from offering solutions before fully understanding the problem.
whyNot.3: This minimises her distress, which NICE warns against.

B.q: Tom, 27, with BPD, is about to move from one community team to another. What does CG78 advise?
options: Transfer him quickly to limit dependency
Discuss and phase the change in advance
Avoid telling him until the date is set
Close his case before the new team starts
B.why: CG78 1.1.6.1: endings and transitions may evoke strong reactions; discuss changes carefully beforehand and make them structured and phased, with crisis access during the transition.

whyNot.3: A gap in care leaves him without crisis access.

B.q: Grace, 35, with BPD, has been admitted to an acute ward twice in the past 6 months. What does NICE recommend?
options: Refuse any further admission
Start a long-term antipsychotic
Discharge her to her GP's care
Arrange a formal CPA review
B.why: CG78 1.4.1.4: arrange a formal CPA review for people with BPD admitted twice or more in the previous 6 months.

whyNot.0: Blanket refusal of admission is exclusion and may be unsafe.
whyNot.1: Antipsychotics are not used long term for BPD.
whyNot.2: Discharge does not address the pattern of crises.

C.q: On the ward, Kayla, 22, with BPD, tells Nurse Ben he is the only nurse who understands her and that the others are cruel. What is the best response?
options: Agree to be her one point of contact on the ward
Stay warm, avoid sides, and share with the team
Report the other nurses to the ward manager now
Tell her she is manipulating the staff team
C.why: This may be splitting. The best response is warm, non-judgemental and boundaried: avoid taking sides, discuss with the team for a consistent approach, and use supervision (CG78 1.1.8.2).

whyNot.0: Becoming the 'good' nurse reinforces the split and is unsustainable.
whyNot.2: Acting on one account without exploring it divides the team.
whyNot.3: Labelling her as manipulative is stigmatising and damages trust.

C.q: Maria, 29, has BPD and moderate depression. Her GP asks whether medication has any role. What is correct under CG78?
options: Medication may treat comorbid depression
Medication should be avoided in all cases
An antipsychotic should be started long term
Several drugs together give the best control
C.why: CG78 1.3.5.3: drug treatment may be considered for comorbid conditions such as depression, while not being used specifically for BPD itself.

whyNot.1: Comorbid conditions can be treated with medication.
whyNot.2: Antipsychotics are not used for medium- or long-term BPD treatment.
whyNot.3: Polypharmacy is not recommended; NICE favours a single drug in crises.

C.q: Zoe, 26, with BPD, is in crisis with suicidal thoughts but no plan, and has support at home. The team discusses admission. What should happen first under CG78?
options: Admit her to an acute ward for 6 weeks
Detain her under section 2 as a precaution
Discharge with a leaflet and GP follow-up
Refer to the crisis and home treatment team
C.why: CG78 1.4.1.1: before considering acute admission, refer to a crisis resolution and home treatment team or other local alternative.

whyNot.0: Admission is considered after alternatives and with an agreed length and purpose.
whyNot.1: Detention needs MHA criteria, not precaution.
whyNot.2: Discharge with a leaflet does not respond to a crisis.

reteach.title: Hope, consistency, no exclusion
reteach.question: What does good care for someone with BPD look like?

blocks.body: Offer hope and a reliable, consistent relationship. Do not exclude anyone because of the diagnosis or self-harm. Treat with psychological therapy, not drugs for BPD itself. In crisis: use the plan, validate, explore alternatives to admission, agree follow-up.

explain.body: People with BPD should not be excluded from any health or social care service because of their diagnosis or self-harm. Work with hope and optimism, aware of past rejection, trauma and stigma.

test.q: A team proposes not accepting referrals of people with BPD who self-harm. What does NICE say?
options: This is acceptable if a crisis line exists
This is acceptable for repeat self-harm
Exclusion on these grounds is not allowed
This is acceptable with GP agreement
test.why: CG78 1.1.1.1: people with BPD should not be excluded from any health or social care service because of their diagnosis or because they have self-harmed.

whyNot.0: A crisis line does not justify exclusion.
whyNot.1: Repeated self-harm is not grounds for exclusion.
whyNot.3: GP agreement does not change the NICE principle.

explain.body: No drugs for BPD itself or its symptoms; no medium- or long-term antipsychotics. Treat comorbid conditions. Crisis: one drug, low side-effect and misuse potential (e.g. sedative antihistamine), usually stopped within 1 week.

items.label: drug at a time in crisis

test.q: Which type of drug does CG78 give as an example for short-term use in a BPD crisis?
options: Long-acting benzodiazepine
Sedative antihistamine
Depot antipsychotic
Tricyclic antidepressant
test.why: CG78: choose a drug with a low side-effect profile, low addictive potential and low misuse potential, such as a sedative antihistamine (unlicensed; informed consent needed).

whyNot.0: Benzodiazepines carry dependence and misuse risks.
whyNot.2: Long-term antipsychotics are not used for BPD.

explain.body: Psychological treatment within a structured service. Consider comprehensive DBT for women where reducing self-harm is a priority. No brief interventions under 3 months for BPD outside a structured, supervised service.

test.q: What does CG78 say about psychological interventions lasting less than 3 months for BPD?
options: They are the first-line choice for BPD itself
They suit people with BPD who are in a crisis
They are not used outside a structured service
They are best delivered by GPs in primary care
test.why: CG78 1.3.4.4: do not use brief psychological interventions (less than 3 months) specifically for BPD or its individual symptoms outside a service with the structured characteristics set out in 1.3.4.3 (shared theoretical approach, structured care, therapist supervision).

whyNot.0: NICE does not make brief interventions a first-line treatment for BPD.
whyNot.1: Crisis care follows the crisis plan (1.3.7.1); it is separate from structured therapy.
whyNot.3: Delivery by GPs is not the issue; the 3-month duration and service structure are.

explain.body: Refer to crisis resolution and home treatment first. Consider admission for crises with significant risk that other services cannot manage, or MHA detention. Agree length and purpose in advance. CPA review if admitted twice or more in 6 months.

test.q: When a person with BPD is admitted, what does CG78 say should be agreed in advance?
options: A ban on any future admissions
Daily PRN sedation for the stay
Transfer to a secure unit later
Its length and purpose
test.why: CG78 1.4.1.3: involve the person, base the decision on a joint understanding of benefits and harms, and agree the length and purpose of admission in advance.

whyNot.0: Future admissions are decided on need.
whyNot.1: Routine sedation is not part of the plan.
whyNot.2: Secure care is not a default.
